The post Universities cannot leave social mobility to their widening participation teams alone appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Jon Datta, Head of University Access Programmes, Student Digital Strategy and University Sector Engagement at the Sutton Trust.

Universities play a crucial role in driving social mobility, but this work can’t be successful if teams are working in silos.

A university can run an excellent summer school and still put avoidable barriers in the way of the students it wants to recruit. Committed staff running outreach programmes can change what a young person thinks is possible, yet that student may then face an admissions policy they can’t decipher, an accommodation deposit they can’t afford or a placement they can’t fit around paid work. Different teams make decisions for different reasons. The student still has to live with the combined result.

Universities put considerable effort into helping students navigate institutions. We should be more willing to change the things that make those institutions difficult to navigate.

This is one of the arguments behind the Sutton Trust’s new best practice guide for universities. It draws on research, our programme delivery and practice from across the sector. There is a great deal worth sharing; however, even a strong intervention will achieve less if other university practices work against it.

An outreach team can help a young person make an ambitious application. It usually can’t change a department’s entry requirements. It can explain financial support but can’tcontrol when that support reaches a student’s bank account. It can introduce professional opportunities without being able to make them affordable. Widening participation teams shouldn’t be left to work around university policies that limit students’ chances of success.

Universities should also make better use of the insights outreach staff gain through their work. Programme teams hear pupils’ questions, discuss concerns with families and see where schools struggle to get answers. That knowledge should inform admissions, communications and student support. Helping someone through a difficult process should also prompt a conversation about whether the process needs to change.

The institution needs to adapt

Access work helps young people understand how university works. Students need good information, academic preparation and opportunities to explore their choices. The problem comes when universities treat every difficulty as something students must learn to overcome, even when the institution could remove the barrier.

If applicants repeatedly misunderstand a contextual admissions policy, universities should examine both the policy and how they explain it. If students arrive unfamiliar with academic conventions, those conventions should be taught within their courses. If a placement means paying for travel or accommodation while losing income from an existing job, universities need to address those costs as well as help students secure the opportunity.

The same applies to belonging. Universities can invest in mentoring and welcome activities while still leaving students unable to afford ordinary course and social experiences. Feeling included is difficult when taking part costs money you do not have.

These are choices about how a university operates. They belong in discussions about social mobility just as much as outreach targets do.

That is why the guide covers admissions, transition, student success and progression into employment or postgraduate study. Antony Moss’s new HEVA proposal for The Post-18 Project adds to this debate by considering continuation, completion and attainment together. It keeps students who leave without completing their course in the picture when assessing attainment, rather than looking only at those who finish.

Universities need to understand where and why disadvantaged students leave their courses as well as how those who graduate perform. Identifying the gap is the starting point. The guide considers what universities can change in response.

Responsibility beyond the widening participation team

‘Whole-provider approach’ is now familiar language, but it can also conceal a lack of agreement about who will do what.

If a university has committed to improving continuation, which academic departments and services are expected to change their practice? Who can approve those changes? What happens if the work is not done?

Senior endorsement and good data matter. They need to lead to decisions about who will act, what will change and how the work will be funded. In England, the commitments universities make in their access and participation plans should shape how departments teach, services support students and leaders allocate funding. The arrangements differ across the UK, but universities everywhere need to show how their plans change students’ day-to-day experience.

Responsibility cannot simply be handed back to the widening participation team under a more expansive job description. Where finance, accommodation, academic departments and careers influence an outcome, their leaders need clear responsibilities for improving it.

There are real limits to what institutions can do. Universities can’t make up for inadequate maintenance support or close school attainment gaps on their own. Their financial pressures make difficult trade-offs unavoidable. Embedding social mobility across an institution still requires investment in specialist expertise and student support. Those pressures only make it more important to check whether decisions in one part of the university are undermining investment in another.

Outreach itself needs the same scrutiny. Universities should know which barrier an intervention addresses, who misses out, whether support continues and what changes for participants. Attendance and positive feedback are useful but they are not enough to establish whether an intervention achieves its aims.

The quality of delivery matters as much as good prgrammme design. Practitioners shape who gets reached and what participants experience. They need professional development, opportunities to learn from one another and time to apply that learning.

The guide offers practical advice and examples. Universities will need to judge what fits, evaluate their approach and change it where necessary. That scrutiny should extend to the institutional decisions that shape students’ opportunities.

Ask your widening participation team where students keep running into barriers. Then ask why it is still their job to work around them.

title: Dreams on hold: The 'frustrating' education limbo facing teenage asylum seekers
summary: Young refugees describe their frustration at the lack of access to education for older teenagers who come to Northern Ireland to live
full_text:
In war-torn Gaza, 16-year-old Mona was able to receive more education than she says she's currently able to get in Northern Ireland.

That is because, as a refugee or asylum seeker aged 16, she is not automatically able to enter school or college in Northern Ireland.

At present, the legal age until which education is compulsory is 16.

But that can leave young people like Mona who have fled conflict to come to Northern Ireland, with no automatic right to education.

BBC News NI has asked the Department of Education and the Department for the Economy for comment.

Mona came to Northern Ireland from Gaza with her family, including her younger siblings.

"I came here to continue the education and be safe here," she said.

"In Gaza I studied online, because of the war."

When Mona arrived she was 15 and did not speak English, though she has learned English since.

She initially attended school in Coleraine, but since her family moved to Belfast she has not been able to get a place in school or college.

"I feel stressed because I cannot find anything for me," she said.

"I would like to study nursing... Because I want to go back to Gaza and help the people in Gaza.

"We are still children and we need education and support."

Sara, 19, who came to Northern Ireland from Sudan in 2024 faced similar frustration.

She received qualifications in Sudan, but although she wants to be a doctor she has been unable to get a university place to study medicine.

"When I came and I tried to get into university they said that as I am a refugee my qualifications would not suffice," she said.

"I had to get the same qualifications as students in Northern Ireland which can be quite frustrating."

Sara speaks very good English but had to wait a year to be admitted to Further Education (FE) College to study A-Levels.

Like Mona, Sara has received some help and support from Anaka Women's Collective, a community organisation which provides support for asylum seekers.

Anaka has previously called for a specialist education programme for those aged 16-24 who come to Northern Ireland as asylum seekers and refugees.

Hani, 20, from Kurdistan and 22-year-old Hossam from Sudan both previously contributed to a report called Stranded Dreams, which outlined the problems older teenagers who were asylum seekers could face when trying to access education.

Both want to set up their own businesses but both are frustrated that little has changed since the Stranded Dreams report was released over a year ago.

Hani has been living in Northern Ireland for four years, and as she was 16 at the time she came her younger siblings could start school but she could not.

Although she registered for English for Speakers of Other Languages (ESOL) classes she had to wait two years before a place was available.

That has delayed her being able to enter classes to take GCSE courses.

"Personally I would love to study a course in business and marketing," she said.

"Young people that have arrived in this country need to have a fair opportunity as other young people in this country.

"Whenever me, my friends and young people come to this country we are starting from zero and we need a pathway to walk in."

Hossam, who has been living in Northern Ireland for three years, feels the same.

"It's surprising, it's really hard to continue in education," he said.

"I really want to be a businessman and fashion designer also."

"So that's my dream and it's really hard to do it here."

The Northern Ireland Executive published a Refugee Integration Strategy in 2025, external to help refugees and asylum seekers integrate into Northern Ireland.

While it aimed to help asylum seekers and refugees "to achieve their full potential" it did not include any specific commitments to provide better access to education for older teenagers.

title: Colleges are cutting administrative jobs — and critics say that’s a good thing

The post Colleges are cutting administrative jobs — and critics say that’s a good thing appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
It was in the quiet of the summer when a new president at Louisiana State University said the school would lay off 25 administrators, including several who were high in the campus hierarchy, and shift the savings to faculty hiring and research.

“Transformational change,” the president, Wade Rousse, called it. He was “streamlining operations and finding efficiencies so the university can focus on” its faculty.

The move got limited attention outside Baton Rouge. But similar layoffs have been happening at universities and colleges nationwide in what may be a little-noticed tipping point in U.S. higher education.

A decades-long increase in the number of employees on campuses who don’t actually teach — disparaged by critics as “administrative bloat” — is starting to reverse, new data suggests.

The number of noninstructional employees at U.S. universities and colleges — the many people on campuses who don’t actually teach — fell last year more than it has at any time in at least the last decade, according to the College and University Professional Association for Human Resources, or CUPA-HR.

And while the newly reported CUPA-HR figures cover only through the end of 2025, universities and colleges have continued to lay off noninstructional employees since then.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

Another source, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, now projects “limited employment growth” for postsecondary administrators, which it says will be slower than for other occupations.

There are several caveats to these clues.

The CUPA-HR survey is limited to the roughly 1,000 public and nonprofit universities and colleges that agreed to participate, for instance. The association cautioned against generalizing across the large variety of higher education institutions; noted that past downturns in staffing often have been followed by increases; and said it might be too early to draw conclusions about trends.

But it shouldn’t come as a surprise that universities are resorting to layoffs across their workforces as they try to lower spending in the face of domestic and international student enrollment declines and federal funding cuts, said Kevin McClure, professor of higher education and chair of the Department of Educational Leadership at the University of North Carolina Wilmington.

“Institutions are shrinking. Some are closing. Some simply have fewer students, so are having to contract,” McClure said. “Those types of situations are often where layoffs are experienced or reorganizations happen.”

Related: Is your college in trouble? Use Hechinger’s College Financial Health Tracker to find out

Since it’s typically harder to eliminate faculty than staff because of tenure and student demand for particular majors, he said, the newest layoffs are most likely to affect “employees and staff who aren’t as protected.”

Among administrators laid off at Louisiana State were the chief financial officer; a vice president who handled discrimination complaints; and 16 writers, video producers and photographers in the marketing and communications office.

The University of Utah has announced it will eliminate as many as 855 noninstructional positions over the next year. The University of Minnesota cut 230 noninstructional jobs through layoffs and attrition. The University of Maryland laid off 84 staffers, eliminated vacant jobs and froze hiring.

Private, nonprofit universities and colleges of all sizes also have been trimming their administrative ranks. Johns Hopkins University laid off 110 workers and imposed a hiring freeze. The New School in New York City shed 68 noninstructional employees. At Baker University in Kansas, 21 staff positions were eliminated, 27 others were frozen and the president and other administrators took pay cuts. Emerson College in Boston laid off 12 administrators.

Related: As international enrollment falls, U.S. students face program cuts and higher prices

Even Harvard University eliminated 165 noninstructional jobs, including the director of its writing center.

In most of these cases, the numbers represent small fractions of the noninstructional workforce, which accounts for more than half of all employees on campuses. But “it’s encouraging that there are any cuts at all,” said Peter Wood, president of the conservative National Association of Scholars, which has been critical of administrative bloat and of diversity, equity and inclusion offices, many of which are among those now being stripped of staff.

There have been decades of increases in the numbers of noninstructional employees, attracting criticism at the highest levels and on social media accounts devoted entirely to making fun of higher education’s middle managers.

“Colleges began to see themselves as providing this very broad suite of services, all of which were personnel-intensive,” Wood said — athletics, housing, dining, security, transportation, mental health counseling, disability support, antidiscrimination efforts, information technology, data collection, fundraising, sustainability.

Some of these functions were expanded as students showed up who were not prepared for college-level work and needed more help. Some were in response to real or perceived demands from consumers for amenities that required additional staff, or were driven by intensifying competition and the race to rise up the college rankings. Institutions also contend that their ever-growing workforces were required to comply with government red tape, though that has proven not to be as big a factor as they’ve said.

The administrative workforce “just grew and grew” — often, Wood said, at the expense of academic functions.

In the process, administrative bloat became “one of those rare issues that unites critics of higher education with faculty members,” said Robert Kelchen, head of the Department of Educational Leadership and Policy Studies at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who has studied it.

Related: Business, government and education leaders try to reinvent college from scratch

A faculty committee convened at Yale University to consider why higher education has lost so much public trust cited administrative bloat as one of the reasons. It said that even determining how many administrators there were at Yale “proved remarkably difficult.” That in itself was a finding, the committee said in its report, released in April. The university “should be able to answer a straightforward question: What share of its resources is devoted to its core academic functions, and what share is not?”

Universities and colleges have “layers of bloated administration” for which “students and taxpayers are forced to foot the bill,” U.S. Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent told a White House roundtable last year. “Students, families and taxpayers are being asked to pay more and more each year to support rising institutional and administrative expenditures that often have little to do with actual learning.”

The number of noninstructional employees on campuses is hard to definitively connect with what students pay. Another analysis of federal data, by the American Council of Trustees and Alumni, or ACTA, however, shows that administrative costs per student at public universities have generally been falling since their last peak, which came just before the Covid-19 pandemic. That analysis covers the period through 2024, the most recent for which the figure is available.

“This seems really like a very stark correction,” said Armand Alacbay, ACTA’s chief of staff and senior vice president of strategy.

Gallup surveys find that fewer than 4 in 10 Americans have confidence in higher education, down from nearly 6 in 10 in 2015; cost edges out perceived political agendas as the top reason, Alacbay noted.

Related: Once globally preeminent, U.S. universities are sliding into decline

“That’s what’s really animating this whole discussion of administrative bloat, is the price of the product reaching an unsustainable level,” he said.

The number of full-time administrators per 100 students at the top 200 universities that award doctoral degrees increased 39 percent from 1993 to 2007 — more than twice as much as the number of students or faculty — according to one widely cited 2010 report by the conservative Goldwater Institute.

Another study picked up the trail in 2012 and looked at 1,529 public and private four-year colleges and universities. It found that administrative staffing continued to grow faster than instructional staffing through at least 2018, even after colleges and universities responded to the 2008 recession by promising to cut costs, and during a period when enrollment was declining.

Universities say their nonfaculty staff include employees in such areas as fundraising and sustainability, meaning they presumably raise or save money. Many others are in student services or provide technology support.

There are indications that some schools are cutting employees who provide those functions, too, potentially resulting in fewer support services for students.

The University of Southern California has laid off academic advisers. The University of California, Los Angeles, cut 27 information technology workers. Indiana University Bloomington laid off 13 IT staffers.

Higher education should be thoughtful about where it’s making cuts, said McClure, the University of North Carolina professor.

Criticism of administrators “paints things in broad brush strokes,” he said. “Let’s be specific. What positions are we actually talking about that we need or don’t need? We should have that conversation.”

Universities and colleges “are in a different era now,” McClure said. “And it’s going to require a different kind of staffing.”

title: Students Increasingly Consider Politics in Choosing a College
summary:
Students Increasingly Consider Politics in Choosing a College Susan H. Greenberg Tue, 10/13/2026 - 03:00 AM The latest iteration of the Art & Science Group poll finds that more students on both the left and the right are ruling out institutions based on the political climate of their states. Byline(s) Susan H. Greenberg Students Increasingly Consider Politics in Choosing a College
Susan H. Greenberg Tue, 10/13/2026 - 03:00 AM

The latest iteration of the Art & Science Group poll finds that more students on both the left and the right are ruling out institutions based on the political climate of their states.

Byline(s)
Susan H. Greenberg
full_text:
Political considerations play a growing role in students’ college-going decisions, according to a new student poll by the Art & Science Group. More than a third (34 percent) of respondents surveyed over the summer said they ruled out a school based solely on the politics of its state, up from 28 percent in 2024 and 24 percent in 2023. Another 12 percent said politics played some role in their higher ed thinking, even if it didn’t change where they ultimately applied or enrolled.

The poll’s new iteration was intended to show whether the 2024 results “were really bound to the runup to the presidential election and the high-volume things coming out of the political sphere,” said David Strauss, co-founder and principal at the Art & Science Group. The new findings indicate “it wasn’t a blip” connected to Donald Trump’s re-election: “It has gone from more than a quarter of students in 2024 to a third of students now in 2026, so that phenomenon is increasing in intensity.”

The findings underscore that “we’re segregating ourselves even more into our own bubble, and we’re doing it younger,” he said. “That worries me.”

The poll also zeroed in on when during the college application process politics impacted students’ choices, with findings similar to 2024. Of students who said they ruled out a college due to politics, nearly three-fourths (73 percent) said it shaped their thinking early on about institutions they might be interested in, 59 percent said politics influenced their decisions about where to apply, 25 percent said they considered it in comparing admissions offers and 13 percent said it helped them determine where to enroll.

“The most intensive role politics is playing is when students are deciding what schools to look into,” Strauss said. “In other words, the colleges may never even see these kids or have an opportunity to try to convince them of something. Those are big impediments for institutions.”

Students who ruled out colleges because of politics looked at both the institutions themselves and the states where they were located. Over 70 percent said they had evaluated specific colleges and universities, and nearly half cited states or regions.

The survey was administered twice during the 2025–26 admissions cycle: once to 1,347 U.S. high school seniors between February and March of 2026, around when they were deciding where to apply, and again to 1,547 graduates in the summer, after they knew where they were going. Across both rounds, 45 percent of respondents identified as white and 55 percent as BIPOC or AAPI, while 58 percent identified as female and 41 percent as male.

Though the breakdown of their political leanings wasn’t included in the report, Strauss told Inside Higher Ed that 20 percent of respondents identified as conservative or very conservative and 34 percent as liberal or very liberal. Another 38 percent described themselves as moderate and 8 percent said they weren’t sure where they stood.

According to the report, more than 15 percent of conservative-leaning students said they ruled out attending college in three states: California, Colorado and New York. Meanwhile, more than 15 percent of liberal-leaning students eliminated institutions in Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas.

Strauss said across the surveys, liberal-leaning students have tended to be “more discerning” in enumerating their reasons for rejecting certain institutions. “Larger portions of liberal-leaning students have talked about reproductive rights and LGBTQ rights, et cetera, and the conservative leaning kids will talk about ‘too Democratic’ or ‘too liberal,’” he said.

But he noted that colleges have some control in overcoming their state’s reputation.

“You can do your best to be the oasis in a state and make it known. So, if you’re a school in California, and a student thinks California is too liberal, you can try to be a place where there are different voices being heard,” he said. “The other thing you can do is have a reason to be a place that the student would want to be more than he or she doesn’t want to be in a state with those politics.”

title: A Student Aid Expert Peels Back the Curtain on College Financing
summary:
A Student Aid Expert Peels Back the Curtain on College Financing Johanna Alonso Tue, 10/13/2026 - 03:00 AM After over a decade studying how much students pay for college, Phil Levine has turned his expertise into a practical guide for prospective students and their families. Byline(s) Johanna Alonso A Student Aid Expert Peels Back the Curtain on College Financing
Johanna Alonso Tue, 10/13/2026 - 03:00 AM

After over a decade studying how much students pay for college, Phil Levine has turned his expertise into a practical guide for prospective students and their families.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
If you care about cost transparency in higher education, the name Phil Levine might be familiar to you. The Wellesley economist, who for the past 15 years has studied the gap between the prices colleges advertise and what students actually pay after discounts, is one of the most outspoken voices on the issue of college cost transparency. He’s also spearheading solutions; he founded MyinTuition, a nonprofit now owned by the College Board that provides simple cost-calculation tools to colleges using their internal data, so prospective students can calculate how much their education would actually cost.

But for 15 years, that work has been aimed mostly at higher ed change makers: those who can influence the price of college and the way that information is communicated. Last month, Levine released his first book for student, families and college counselors, drawing not only on the findings of his research but also on his years of experience working with college leaders and financial aid officers to spill the behind-the-scenes secrets of paying for college.

Levine hopes Hidden Tuition: An Insider’s Guide to College Pricing and Financial Aid (University of Chicago Press) will help prospective students understand how to pay for college, as well as some of the mechanics of how the financial aid system works.

He sat down with Inside Higher Ed to discuss the book. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Q: What is the niche you were hoping to fill with this book?

A: I’ve written many things in the past on higher education finance and college pricing. Usually it’s to a professional audience, and that’s great, except that the people who really need the information are people who are considering going to college or helping people go to college. So, I wanted to write a book that was targeted at parents and students and college counselors. So we’re taking all the things that I’ve learned over the many years of working on the problem and communicating it in a way that is accessible to all types of readers.

Q: At what point in your career studying college costs did you realize that a book like this was needed?

A: Well, let’s start from the beginning. I’ve been teaching at Wellesley College for 35 years. I spent 20 of them not even remotely thinking about college cost, and how I got interested in it was that I have kids, too. My kids got to be college age, or approaching college age, and I’m an economist, I make a good living; I don’t make a fortune, but I make a good living. I’ve been saving for college since the day my kids were born, and by the time they were in their teenage years, I just wondered, “Have I saved enough? Am I going to be eligible for any financial aid? What’s it really going to cost me?” And that’s when I realized, OK, wait, something’s wrong here. Because I couldn’t figure it out. Given my background, if it’s a struggle for me, it’s probably a struggle for a lot of other people, too.

The tools that I developed are sort of direct [tools for] trying to figure out how much it costs. And the book is sort of like, “Let’s understand the system and think about, what does it mean for me? And how does it affect my decision?”

Q: What specific facets of higher education pricing did you want to be sure to get into that you don’t think are well represented in other resources?

A: There are many, but the most basic element of the problem is the focus on the sticker price. There’s plenty of data out there that shows that families overestimate what they say college is going to cost them, that they typically focus exclusively on a sticker price. And then there’s research that shows that most people don’t pay the sticker price. And then the question arises, “Well, what do they pay? And how do you figure it out?” There’s lots of issues that are involved, but that’s the most important one.

Q: You get into sort of this broader picture of how college pricing works in the first part of the book, beyond what would seem to be immediately relevant to students and families. Why was that something you wanted to include?

A: There’s a public perception that colleges sort of make up these prices, that they want to bring in as much revenue as they possibly can. That’s just not the way the market works. Colleges are businesses, too; they have expenses. Revenue from students is certainly one way that they help pay those expenses; at some institutions, that’s a larger share than elsewhere. But they need to pay their bills, and so you need to generate enough revenue to pay bills. On the other hand, they can’t charge as much as they want because people aren’t willing to pay an unlimited amount. So, as a business, making a business decision, how do you set up the pricing system that generates the revenue that you need to pay your bills in a way that families are willing to pay?

That’s not a simple task, and pretty much every financial aid administrator I think I’ve ever talked to would be thrilled to be able to charge nothing to everyone, especially lower-income families. It’s just not feasible, because it’s still a business. It’s important to understand, from the institution’s perspective, why are they making the decisions that they make? Because that influences how the system is set up, which influences how you navigate the system.

Q: On that note, what are some pieces of advice that you thought were important about navigating the system? Again, especially advice that you thought was not included in some other prominent sources.

A: The importance of price shopping is critical. And price shopping is not necessarily focused on the sticker price, because you’re most likely not going to pay that. Some schools rely on merit aid in their financial aid systems. It’s great to receive merit aid, and it’s great to feel the admiration and respect that a merit award provides. But it’s really just a pricing mechanism. So ultimately, how much merit you get is not the question. It’s, how much are you going to have to pay? It’s not uncommon for me to hear people say, in casual conversation, “Oh yeah, my child decided to go to school X because they offered them a $20,000 merit award.” What instantly goes through my head is “Well, that’s great, but how much are you going to pay?” That’s what matters.

Q: Your own research is very prominent throughout and inspired how you wrote the book. Tell me about where and how you decided to incorporate that work into this resource.

A: The book is not written as an academic book, so there aren’t references and citations. But a good amount of it is based on things that I’ve learned through my own research and the research of the people that I work with as an economist. Specifically in terms of recent research, just last week I released a paper on free tuition [programs]. That’s in the book. There’s research that I’ve released six months ago on, how extensive is the use of merit aid awards. There’s certainly research in there [about] what people ultimately pay at different income levels, which is very difficult to find elsewhere.

And there’s everything that I’ve learned from the MyinTuition tools that I’ve generated over the years. The learning from that isn’t necessarily academic research, but I can’t even tell you how much I’ve learned from working with the colleges that I work with in terms of how they do the things that they do, why they do the things that they do, how that impacts the prices that they charge families with different financial resources. Getting sort of under the hood of, why do they think the things that they think?

Q: What are some of the takeaways from that that you included in the book?

A: I’m actually on a nonprofit board for college savings where the people on the board are financial aid administrators and admissions professionals. And it’s amazing what you can learn at lunch. They talk about the things that they think about and what their concerns are and how they navigate the world in sort of an informal way. And what’s interesting for me about it is that, as an economist, we’re having normal lunchtime conversation, but in the back of my head, it’s getting translated into the economics of how higher education works.

Q: I assume that the process of publishing this, rolling it out and trying to get it to the right audience has been very different for you. What has that been like? How can you get it into the hands of students and families for years to come?

A: I’d love to be able to do that. It’s definitely a different marketing issue. If I write a report at Brookings [Institute] about free tuition programs, and Inside Higher Ed picks it up, which they did on Monday [Sept. 28], that’s going to the right audience. I know how to do that. But how do you communicate with a broader audience? I’m an economics professor. That’s not what I normally do. So, I’m doing podcasts and webinars that are more public-facing. I’m doing a podcast in a few weeks for financial advisers, [who can be] an important source of information for parents.

It’s a very different exercise. The MyinTuition work that I’ve done has been advantageous because there are marketing efforts there, too. So I definitely have gotten greater exposure to communication strategies in ways that it happened earlier in my career. That’s not something they teach you in graduate school.

title: Career Readiness Should Be Developmental, Not Episodic
summary:
Career Readiness Should Be Developmental, Not Episodic joshua.m.kim@d… Tue, 10/13/2026 - 03:00 AM A guest post by James DeVaney. Byline(s) James DeVaney Career Readiness Should Be Developmental, Not Episodic
joshua.m.kim@d… Tue, 10/13/2026 - 03:00 AM

A guest post by James DeVaney.

Byline(s)
James DeVaney
full_text:
This fall, two of my nephews began their first year at the University of Michigan. I spoke with them at length as they contemplated where to attend, and ultimately they chose Michigan—the same place where, many years ago, I began my own undergraduate journey.

As they embark on their own learning journeys, I am struck by how different their experiences will be from mine. They will have more ways to explore their interests, encounter employers, build capabilities and connect learning with work. They will also face a more complex set of choices—and a world of work that will change dramatically between their first day and graduation.

As I consider what I hope they will experience over the next four years, I also think about what universities owe them and every student: not simply more opportunities, but a developmental journey that enables students to make increasingly informed decisions and learn from their choices.

In the first column in this series, I argued that career readiness cannot wait until graduation. Educators, employers and university leaders responded with examples of how they are already connecting learning and work. Their responses reinforced a central point worthy of further reflection: An early encounter with an authentic problem does more than prepare a student for a future job. It can transform how that student experiences everything that follows.

A student who has seen disciplinary knowledge applied in the world returns to the classroom with different questions. Concepts acquire context. Productive struggle gains purpose. The student begins to understand where their learning might lead and how they might contribute.

That suggests a more ambitious goal than ensuring every student secures an internship. What if students encountered dozens of progressively challenging opportunities to connect learning and work throughout their undergraduate education?

Career readiness should not be an assortment of disconnected programs clustered around graduation. It should be developmental: Students should explore possibilities, exercise increasing agency, tackle authentic problems and learn to explain and reconsider their choices.

One Internship Can’t Do It All

Internships are extraordinarily valuable. They give students meaningful experience, professional relationships, greater confidence and a clearer vision of where they want to go next. But not every student has access to one.

Strada Education Foundation’s 2025 State Opportunity Index shows that 43 percent of seniors at four-year institutions reported having at least one paid work-based learning experience. Access depends on time, geography, financial flexibility, confidence, prior experience and social capital.

The supply of conventional opportunities also does not approach student demand. The Business–Higher Education Forum estimates that 8.2 million students sought internships or similar experiences in 2023, but approximately 4.6 million could not access the opportunities they wanted, according to its 2026 analysis “Lost in Translation: Navigating the Work-Integrated Learning Landscape.”

But even excellent internships remain a single experience. Students need repeated opportunities to test their interests, encounter different forms of work, apply knowledge in new settings and make progressively better-informed choices.

The goal should be to place internships within a much richer continuum of career-connected learning. That continuum could include research, simulations, client projects, campus employment, entrepreneurial ventures, industry challenges, community-based work, student organizations, online learning, open-source projects, portfolio development and interdisciplinary competitions.

Many of these opportunities already exist across our institutions. Yet students frequently experience them as isolated activities rather than connected parts of their development.

From Visibility to Agency

Early on, faculty can help undergraduates see how disciplinary knowledge is applied in professional settings. They might demonstrate how a concept informs a public debate, professional practice, research question, organizational decision, creative work or community challenge. Alumni and practitioners can make unseen opportunities visible, showing how disciplinary thinking applies in unfamiliar settings.

As students progress, they should gain greater agency to explore possibilities by investigating a field, interviewing professionals, comparing organizational approaches, identifying a worthy problem or determining how a particular capability is used across different sectors.

Students can then encounter more career possibilities, test their assumptions and make more informed choices—including the choice to change direction.

Over time, the ambiguity and stakes should increase. Advanced students should encounter problems without obvious answers. They should decide which information matters, determine what can be trusted, weigh competing priorities, choose among imperfect alternatives and accept responsibility for the consequences of their decisions.

Agency becomes meaningful when students have room to make consequential choices—and when the work is difficult enough to reveal the limits of what they know. Students should also help shape this developmental journey by identifying which opportunities feel accessible, where connections remain invisible and which institutional processes create unnecessary barriers.

From Choice to Reflective Defense

Greater agency demands greater reflection. After completing authentic work, students should have an opportunity to explain what they decided, why they decided it, what evidence informed their reasoning, which trade-offs they considered and how they responded when their original approach did not work.

They should also be asked, what would you do differently, knowing what you know now?

I think of this as a reflective defense. The purpose is not to prove that every choice was correct. It is to demonstrate the capacity to learn from evidence, feedback and experience—to explain one’s reasoning, acknowledge uncertainty and revise one’s thinking.

The defense could take many forms: an oral examination, portfolio review, written reflection, public presentation, recorded explanation or conversation with faculty, peers and practitioners. It should be designed accessibly and assessed through transparent criteria that emphasize reasoning, evidence, reflection and growth—not confidence, polish or conformity to a single communication style.

At work, the right answer is rarely enough. People must explain how they framed the problem, why they chose their approach, what they learned and how they would adapt as circumstances change.

Experience, evidence and expression reinforce one another.

This connection is especially important in a labor market that increasingly emphasizes durable skills. As Colleen Flaherty recently reported in Inside Higher Ed, Dan Silverburg of Propel K20 argues that claims about critical thinking, communication and adaptability become meaningful to employers when paired with evidence that students have applied those capabilities to real work.

The reflective defense adds another layer by asking students to express what they learned, how they contributed and how their judgment is developing. The experience gives students something consequential to do. Their work provides evidence of their capabilities. Their reflection helps them determine what should come next.

Advice for the Journey Ahead

As I think about my nephews beginning their own undergraduate journeys, this developmental progression suggests some more personal advice.

Do not wait for someone to declare you career-ready. Seek out experiences that let you see how knowledge operates in the world. Try things before you are certain they are right for you. Notice what energizes you and what does not. Ask for feedback. Save the evidence of what you have done. Build relationships with people whose work you want to understand.

Most importantly, learn to explain the choices you make—and to reconsider them without treating a change of direction as failure. The world will change during your four years at Michigan, and so will you. The objective is not to predict that world perfectly or decide your entire future now. It is to become increasingly capable of determining what to do next.

That is what I hope for my nephews. It is also what every student should be able to expect from a university designed for the future.

title: ‘Act five’: National Assembly opens budget debate amid ongoing student protests in France
summary: The French government's budget proposal includes a €1.2 billion increase in funding for the National Education Ministry, as France grapples with one of the highest public deficits in the eurozone.
full_text:
Another major day of demonstrations took place across France on Tuesday, with students and trade unions taking to the streets to protest education conditions and funding as the National Assembly began its debate on the government's budget proposals for 2027.

Teaching unions told Euronews that they were dissatisfied with the government's response to concerns over long school days, overcrowded classrooms, run down facilities, and teacher absences.

"It is clear that the responses that have been provided are inadequate and do not meet the needs set out," Elisabeth Allain-Moreno, secretary-general of SE UNSA, a teachers' union, said.

France's Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced on 8 October that 3,000 available supply teachers would be deployed across more than 500 priority schools by Tuesday in a bid to solve teacher absences.

On Tuesday, he announced that just 35% of the target had been achieved.

"We have a generation that is articulating demands that we identified years ago, which we have been advocating for and were never heard," Morgane Verviers, secretary-general of UNSA Education, told Euronews.

"It's clear that the responses provided are inadequate and don't meet the needs set out," Moreno added.

Budget proposal under fire

The government's budget proposal includes a €1.2 billion increase in funding for the National Education Ministry, as France grapples with one of the highest public deficits in the eurozone.

However, critics say this measure is insufficient, arguing that a 1.6% increase in funding falls short of inflation, which is forecast at 1.8%.

Sabrine Kharbach, a spokesperson for l'Union Etudiante, France's biggest student union, said she felt the government had underestimated students' ability to understand budget matters.

"They believe that students and young people are not aware of the economy and don't understand what's happening. But we truly understand, when we see that there's an additional $400 billion being allocated to the military," Kharbach told Euronews. France's government has allocated a total budget of €413.3 billion to its armed forces for 2024 to 2030 under its Military Programming Law (LPM).

"We have to ask ourselves if they want to invest in death or in the future," she added.

One secondary school student said she felt her generation was not being taken seriously, despite being the "future of France."

"We can't turn a blind eye to issues, especially in secondary schools in the suburbs, which really lack funding," she said.

Swedish activist Greta Thunberg also joined Tuesday's protests, telling the AFP news agency that "young people are not being included in the conversation."

"Our future is being robbed away from us," she added.

Thunberg's visit to France comes after French students' grievance struck a chord with young people across Europe, leading students in Belgium and Italy to stage their own demonstrations over the past week.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed party, was also among those who joined the protests.

Taking to X on 8 October, he declared that the Bastille had been "retaken" after a mass protest on Paris' Place de la Bastille captured audiences worldwide.

Police violence sparks outrage

France's protests and school blockades began in Paris’s suburbs in mid-September, before rapidly spreading nationwide.

While many demonstrations have been peaceful, others have been marred by sideline riots and clashes with police.

Rights groups have accused officers of exercising disproportionate force whilst dealing with protesters following a wave of injuries to students.

According to figures shared by France's Ministry of Justice on Friday, there have been 6,877 arrests since the beginning of the movement, mostly involving minors.

More than 215 students and nearly 800 police officers have also been injured.

title: Why did academics and activists sleep in Telangana schools? | Explainer
summary: Budgetary support for education has declined to a single-digit percentage of the State outlay and has remained so over the past decade
full_text:
The story so far

The state of schools and teaching has been in the spotlight nationally. In Telangana, a collective of academics, bureaucrats and activists known as the Telangana People’s Front was on a 12-day tour of districts in the State to understand and highlight the state of schools called ‘Vidya Bus Yatra’.

Why is this being done now?

Budgetary support for education has declined to a single-digit percentage of the State outlay and has remained so over the past decade. After the formation of the Congress government by A. Revanth Reddy, a Telangana Education Commission was formed under former IAS officer Akunuri Murali to suggest measures to improve the sector. After his two-year term with the commission expired, Mr. Murali quit the commission and has take up cudgels for reform and started the ‘Vidya Bus Yatra’.

Is there a road map for improving schools?

The Telangana Education Commission submitted a 354-page report after visiting 305 institutions over 14 months in all 33 districts. The report has four annexures that are draft Bills that lay out a clear map to reinforce and rebuild the education sector in Telangana. Also sketched out was a six-phase plan to upgrade the infrastructure at a total cost of ₹31,600 crores, staggered across five years. It also created a checklist on what constitutes a Telangana Foundation School.

A functioning model of the concept is Telangana Public School at Arutla, about 50 km from Hyderabad. The school is a pre-primary to Intermediate facility and offers English-medium education with airy classrooms, a playground, free transport, three meals a day, and sports facilities.

What the ‘Vidya Bus Yatra’ revealed?

Schools without compound walls. Taps without running water. Locked toilets or dysfunctional toilets. In Gattuguddenapalli village, the government school had fewer than 60 students, where the inspiration was a science and Telugu teacher, but one of the children wanted either salt or jaggery to be given to add taste to “Ragi java (millet broth)”.

What is ‘badi nidra’?

The members of Telangana People’s Front not only visited the schools but also slept in them at night to experience in real time the functioning of amenities in the schools. They discovered that Unified District Information System for Education Plus (UDISE+) data that is being updated almost daily for consideration of national ranking does not match the ground reality.

A drinking water tap may be in the school, but how often it functions is different. This is the same issue flagged by the UN report ‘Progress on drinking water, sanitation and hygiene in schools 2015-2025’. The UN report found that 50 million, or five crore, Indian children still lack access to sanitation service in their schools.

Is the infrastructure the only issue?

One of the academics who was part of the bus yatra says that mismanagement of resources with irrational deployment of staff is a big bugbear. “Some schools have excess classrooms, others without enough rooms. All are under the Education Department, but the head of each institution doesn’t want to share the barely functional infrastructure.”

There are schools with 10 teachers where the number of students is 60, and then there are other schools with 50 students and two teachers, where one of them is either on long leave or absent. In multi-grade classrooms, children don’t have space, and students sit in the verandahs,” she said.

What’s the road ahead?

The Telangana People’s Front wants to mobilise parents and society to force the government to act on its proposals to raise spending on education from the current 8.2% to 18%. Make government schools share resources like playgrounds, classrooms, labs, library facilities, etc. Currently, the government spends ₹1,10,00 on each student, according to an estimate. Once the resources are shared, facilities expanded then this cost will drop to ₹55,000, according to a TPF estimate.

title: Why science’s contract with society needs citizens as research partners
summary: While governments, as the patrons, are entitled to establish broad priorities and expectations, they should not use science policy as an excuse to politically micromanage research
full_text:
For hundreds of years, science has operated with a social contract: science develops knowledge that improves the human condition and expands the range of what is possible while society provides public funds, infrastructure, and institutional support. Sustained investments in research have paid dividends to society, in the form of inventions and discoveries, new technologies, and more innovation in general.

Today, this contract is being strained. Governments are increasingly demanding measurable returns from public investments in research while public trust in institutions is reducing. As a result, science can no longer afford to remain an activity conducted largely for society but without society. The next phase of scientific progress must involve citizens as beneficiaries and taxpayers as well as as partners in deciding which questions science should address and how scientific knowledge should be used.

Patrons of science

Curiosity-driven research often produces unexpected discoveries that eventually transform society. Yet governments, as major patrons of science, are increasingly asserting their right to determine where research money should go. There are legitimate reasons for this. Governments are obligated to resolve national priorities because public resources are finite. But governments misstep when their policy-driven management becomes intrusive.

When funding decisions are mainly influenced by short-term political priorities or economic returns, research areas that are not easily measurable, such as parts of the social sciences, humanities, climate research, and fundamental science, become vulnerable to being seen — unjustifiably — as producing too little bang for the buck. Yes, science must serve society, but science also works better when it retains the intellectual freedom required to challenge prevailing assumptions and explore questions whose value may not be immediately apparent.

Governments, as the patrons, are entitled to establish broad priorities and expectations, but they should not use science policy as an excuse to politically micromanage research. But the answer is also not to isolate science further from society. Instead, the answer is in the middle: scientists must build a broader constituency for science by bringing society into the research process.

To achieve this, scientists need compelling narratives about why research matters, and allies across communities, civil society, industry, education, and public institutions.

What citizens know

Inviting citizens into research does not mean replacing scientific expertise with popular opinion. A scientist trained in epidemiology knows considerably more about disease transmission than the average citizen. A climate scientist understands atmospheric processes in ways that a farmer may not. However, the reverse is also true. A farmer may possess knowledge about changing soil behaviour and crop resilience that a scientist in a laboratory may not. A forest-dwelling community may possess detailed knowledge of medicinal plants, forests, and biodiversity that is absent in formal databases.

Scientific knowledge and community knowledge are different — and they can be complementary. The challenge is to bring them together. This is particularly relevant to a country like India, which is one of the world’s most biologically and culturally diverse countries. Indeed, India is too geographically vast and ecologically diverse for professional scientists alone to be able to understand every landscape by themselves. A network of citizens can provide observations across locations and seasons that conventional research is not designed to capture. For instance, a school student studying a butterfly or a birdwatcher recording a migratory species can contribute to ecological knowledge. Citizen science can transform the relationship between the public and scientific institutions.

India’s long tradition of community-based conservation reveals another aspect of this argument. Sacred groves, community forests, germplasm conservation, traditional systems of resource management, and so on demonstrate that local communities have often developed sophisticated ways to understand and protect ecosystems. One of the key success metrics in research is observation, which many local communities excel at. So instead of merely entering a village to collect traditional knowledge and leaving with a publication, researchers can, and should, establish long-term partnerships with communities. Local knowledge bearers should participate in framing research questions, identifying species, help interpret the findings, and decide how knowledge is documented and used.

Rebuilding trust

Under the European Union’s Horizon 2020 programme, citizens from numerous countries participated in developing research priorities. Here, while expert-led foresight exercises tended to emphasise technological advancement, citizens placed greater emphasis on strong communities, health and well-being, education, and local economies. A similar approach in India could have significant implications. Research priorities relating to groundwater, urban pollution, agricultural resilience, coastal erosion, public health, biodiversity, nutrition or climate adaptation, for example, can be developed through structured dialogue among scientists, policymakers, and the most affected communities.

Another compelling reason for citizen participation is trust. Specifically, public trust in governments and institutions is becoming increasingly fragile. Scientists and universities are sometimes portrayed as distant elites disconnected from the concerns of ordinary people. At the same time, misinformation spreads rapidly through social media and emotional narratives can compete successfully with carefully established scientific evidence. The instinctive response is often to communicate more science. But perhaps the deeper problem is a lack of participation and ownership.

People are more likely to support a process when they believe their voices have been heard. They may not agree with every conclusion but they are more likely to accept decisions when the reasoning is transparent and their concerns have been seriously considered. This is particularly important for contentious issues such as climate change, vaccination, genetic modification, artificial intelligence, and biotechnologies. Science cannot promise that every citizen will agree with every scientific conclusion — nor should it. But it can promise a fair opportunity to question, participate, deliberate, and understand.

Humility from scientists

At present, many researchers are trained to design experiments, analyse data, and publish papers but not necessarily to build long-term relationships with communities. That must change. Community engagement should be integrated into research training. Academic recognition should extend beyond publications and citations to include meaningful societal engagement and co-produced research. Funding agencies should also encourage researchers to explain, wherever appropriate, how communities will participate in setting priorities, conducting research, interpreting results and disseminating findings.

To be sure, not every laboratory experiment requires citizen participation. The objective is also not to impose participation mechanically. Public involvement should instead become the default expectation for research with significant societal implications, with researchers explaining why participation is inappropriate when it is not used. Should an emerging technology be deployed rapidly or cautiously? How much privacy should society sacrifice for technological convenience? How should the benefits and risks of artificial intelligence be distributed? How should climate-transition costs be shared? Such questions can benefit enormously from community engagement.

This transformation also requires some humility from scientists. Scientists must learn to listen, be willing to hear uncomfortable questions, acknowledge uncertainties, and recognise the values embedded in their own recommendations. At the same time, the public must recognise that scientific evidence cannot always provide simple answers to complex social questions.

title: ITECA warns Australian policy is “choking” international education and skills pipeline
summary:
Australia’s independent tertiary education sector has accused the government of putting international education and the country’s long-term skills pipeline at risk, as providers grapple with rising costs and tighter policy settings.

The post ITECA warns Australian policy is “choking” international education and skills pipeline appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Independent Tertiary Education Council Australia (ITECA) chief executive Felix Pirie said two registered training organisations (RTOs) had contacted the association in the past week to say they would close by the end of October “as a direct result of government policy decisions”.

“We’d like governments to get off our backs and to stop making every day harder than the one before,” said Pirie.

He pointed to international education’s contribution of almost AUD$55 billion to the economy in 2025, arguing that restrictions on the sector would have consequences beyond education providers.

“The federal government has carelessly taken a hatchet to those jobs and to the communities that support them through education, hospitality and retail,” said Pirie.

ITECA also criticised current student visa settings, claiming the Department of Home Affairs (DHA) is now refusing around one in three offshore higher education visa applications.

Pirie said this increases the risk of “artificially contracting Australia’s fourth-largest export sector”, with potential consequences for GDP and living standards.

He warned the policies could result in the “choking of Australia’s long-term skills pipeline”, particularly across nursing and care, engineering and mining, hospitality, construction and agriculture.

The association also took aim at regulatory pressures, including a Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA) consultation on updated fees and charges due to take effect from January 2027.

However, Pirie welcomed action by the Australian Skills Quality Authority (ASQA) against non-genuine providers.

“Integrity matters,” he said. “As we have seen, when some are not doing the right thing, everyone suffers as regulators are undermined and under-resourced, and the scale of their work becomes overwhelming.

“The result is not that governments seek a better system, rather, they seek a smaller one. That means fewer choices, and dimmer prospects for the learners of the future and for our economies and communities,” said Pirie.

Independent tertiary education doesn’t need a lifeline. Neither do our students. We need to foster ambition, not cut it off at the knees

Felix Pirie, ITECA

“Independent tertiary education doesn’t need a lifeline. Neither do our students. We need to foster ambition, not cut it off at the knees.”

title: They’re Not Lazy: Why Trauma-Informed Teaching Matters in Higher Education

The post They’re Not Lazy: Why Trauma-Informed Teaching Matters in Higher Education appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
I was that student.

I was an adult learner balancing a full-time job, raising children, managing bills, and pursuing a doctoral degree during a global pandemic. Within one year, I lost both of my grandparents. Life was happening in real time—grief, uncertainty, and emotional exhaustion—while the expectation remained unchanged: show up, perform, submit.

But I did not have anything left to give.

In many of my classes, I felt invisible—just a name on a roster, another assignment in the gradebook. Eventually, I had to step away from my program, not because I lacked motivation, but because I lacked capacity.

When I returned, one professor changed everything.

She cared—genuinely.

She reached out. She was patient. She created space for me to be human while still holding me accountable. That experience reshaped how I view teaching. I decided in that moment: I would become the kind of educator I needed when I was struggling.

Now, as an instructor, I see clearly—students are not lazy. They are navigating lives we do not always see.

What Trauma Looks Like in the Online Classroom

Trauma does not always present itself in obvious ways. In higher education—particularly in online learning environments—it often shows up as behavior.

Students:

Apologize excessively for circumstances beyond their control

Disappear instead of communicating

Shut down after missing deadlines or falling short of expectations

Avoid engagement due to fear of judgment or failure

These behaviors are frequently misinterpreted as a lack of effort or disinterest. In reality, they often reflect overwhelm, fear, or survival responses.

As illustrated in the poem “’Cause I Ain’t Got a Pencil” by Joshua T. Dickerson (1991), what appears as unpreparedness is often the result of unseen hardship. Students arrive in our classrooms carrying experiences that shape their ability to participate, perform, and persist.

If we only respond to the behavior, we miss the story behind it.

Equity Is Not the Same as Equality

One of the most common misunderstandings in education is the belief that fairness means treating all students the same.

Equality gives every student the same resources.

Equity recognizes that students are not starting from the same place—and provides what each student needs to succeed.

When we insist on identical expectations without considering individual circumstances, we risk reinforcing inequities rather than addressing them. Trauma-informed teaching is not about lowering standards; it is about removing unnecessary barriers so that students can meet them.

What We Get Wrong as Educators

Too often, higher education equates rigidity with rigor.

We:

Enforce inflexible policies without context

Interpret missed work as laziness

Expect students to “figure it out” independently

Lose sight of our purpose as educators

Over time, the structure of academia can cause us to forget why we began teaching in the first place. Trauma-informed teaching is not an additional responsibility—it is a return to that purpose.

What Trauma-Informed Teaching Looks Like in Practice

Trauma-informed teaching is not theoretical. It is practical, intentional, and immediately applicable.

Here are strategies that consistently work in my classroom:

1. Open, Consistent Communication

From the first day, I tell my students: life happens. Communication matters. Students do not need to overshare, but they do need to keep me informed. When communication is established, support becomes possible.

2. Flexible, Structured Policies

I maintain expectations while allowing flexibility when students communicate. Late work is accepted with accountability. The goal is not perfection—it is persistence.

3. Proactive Outreach

When students disengage or miss assignments, I reach out first. This simple act often re-engages students who might otherwise withdraw completely.

4. Strength-Based Feedback

I use a “sandwich” approach—affirmation, guidance, encouragement. Rather than focusing on what students did wrong, I emphasize how they can improve moving forward. Tone matters. Feedback should build, not break students.

5. Purpose-Driven Motivation

I remind students to remember their “why.” When coursework becomes overwhelming, reconnecting to purpose can sustain effort and resilience.

Why This Matters More in Online Learning

Online learning environments amplify disconnection.

Students:

Lack face-to-face interaction

Are more likely to feel invisible

Can easily misinterpret tone in written communication

Experience increased isolation

In these environments, communication becomes the primary tool for connection. When instructors lead with clarity, empathy, and intentionality, students are more likely to engage and persist.

Tone becomes pedagogy.

What Happens When We Get It Right

When trauma-informed teaching is implemented effectively, the impact is measurable.

Students:

Stay enrolled

Improve academic performance

Communicate more openly

Rebuild confidence

I have had students who failed multiple courses complete mine—not because the content was easier, but because the environment was more accessible.

Research supports this approach. Trauma-informed educational practices have been shown to improve student engagement, retention, and academic outcomes (Carello and Butler 2015; Imad 2021). Additionally, research shows that trauma and stress can significantly impact memory, attention, and overall cognitive functioning, directly affecting a student’s ability to learn (NICABM 2018).

Sometimes, the difference is not the curriculum—it is the connection.

A Question for Educators

For those who believe this approach is not their responsibility, I ask:

What do you want to be remembered for?

Most educators did not enter this profession to enforce policies. They entered it to make an impact. Trauma-informed teaching allows us to reconnect with that purpose.

Conclusion

Students are not showing up empty—they are showing up carrying everything.

When we recognize that—and respond with intention, flexibility, and care—we create learning environments where students can not only succeed academically but continue moving forward in their lives.

They’re not lazy.

They’re navigating life.

And sometimes, what they need most is a professor who sees them.

Dr. Ariel R. Vaughan, PhD, QMHP, is a psychology instructor, published researcher, and trauma-informed educator with a background in counseling and higher education. Drawing from both lived experience and professional practice, she focuses on creating supportive, student-centered learning environments in online and higher-education settings. Her work bridges research and practice by offering practical strategies that improve student engagement, retention, and academic success while recognizing the real-life challenges students navigate.

References

Carello, Janice, and Lisa D. Butler. 2015. “Practicing What We Teach: Trauma-Informed Educational Practice.” Journal of Teaching in Social Work 35 (3): 262–278.

Dickerson, Joshua T. 1991. “’Cause I Ain’t Got a Pencil.”

Imad, Mays. 2021. “A Trauma-Informed Approach to Teaching.” The Chronicle of Higher Education.

National Institute for the Clinical Application of Behavioral Medicine (NICABM). 2018. How Trauma Affects Learning and Behavior.
