full_text:
Artificial Intelligence has rapidly entered teacher preparation programs. Preservice teachers are increasingly using generative AI tools to brainstorm lesson ideas, differentiate instruction, create assessments, draft parent communication, and generate instructional materials (Celik, Dindar, & Jarvela, 2022; Tunjera & Chigona, 2025). In many ways, this shift mirrors earlier waves of educational technology integration: the tools arrive quickly, enthusiasm grows rapidly, and educators work to determine how these technologies can meaningfully support teaching and learning within their individual environments (Cuban, 2018; Violanti, 2023).

But amid this enthusiasm surrounding AI, one issue deserves far more attention in teacher preparation programs: student privacy.

Many preservice teachers have little experience navigating the legal and ethical responsibilities surrounding student data. As a result, they may unknowingly enter personally identifiable information (PII) into public AI systems without understanding the implications. Teacher education programs therefore face an important challenge to not simply teach future educators how to use AI, but to help them understand when AI use becomes inappropriate, unethical, or potentially unlawful within K-12 settings.

The conversation surrounding AI in education cannot focus solely on efficiency or innovation, it must also center on professional responsibility.

The Problem Many Preservice Teachers Do Not Recognize

Today’s teacher candidates are often highly comfortable with digital tools. However, assumptions that they fully understand the implications of these tools are often unfounded (Bennett & Maton, 2010) . Many already use AI informally before entering methods courses or field placements. They may use chatbots to summarize readings, generate discussion questions, or revise writing. Because these tools feel conversational and accessible, it is easy for students to forget that AI platforms are still data systems. This creates a significant concern in teacher preparation that is not being addressed (Tunjera & Chigona, 2025) .

Consider a few common scenarios:

A preservice teacher uploads a struggling student’s writing sample into an AI chatbot and asks for feedback suggestions.

A candidate enters information about a student’s learning disability while seeking differentiation ideas.

A student teacher copies behavioral concerns into an AI platform to generate a parent email draft.

A candidate uploads assessment data to help AI create small-group interventions.

In each case, the preservice teacher may believe they are trying to help students. However, they may also be disclosing protected student information into systems that have not been approved by a school district or institution. Many teacher candidates simply do not realize this is problematic.

Why This Matters in K-12 Education

K-12 educators have long held ethical and legal responsibilities surrounding student records and confidentiality. AI tools do not eliminate those responsibilities.

In New York State, Education Law §2-d establishes protections surrounding the privacy and security of student data (The New York State Senate, 2024) . Similar protections exist nationally through laws such as the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) (Education, 1974) . While teacher candidates do not need to become legal experts, they do need to understand an important principle:

Student information should never be entered into AI systems without careful consideration of privacy, district policy, appropriate legislation, and platform protections.

The challenge is that many public AI tools are not designed specifically for K-12 educational compliance. Some platforms may store prompts, use uploaded information for system improvement, or lack safeguards expected in school environments. Even when names are removed, contextual details may still make students identifiable, particularly in small schools, communities, or specialized classroom environments.

Teacher education programs therefore face a significant task: helping future educators understand not only how to use AI, but when its use may become inappropriate, unethical, or even unlawful in K–12 settings.

Moving Beyond “How to Prompt”

Much of the current AI conversation in higher education focuses on prompting techniques and workflow strategies (Celik, Dindar, & Jarvela, 2022; Lucas, Bem-haja, Zhang, Llorente-Cejudo, & Palacios-Rodriguez, 2025). Those conversations are useful, but they are incomplete. Preservice teachers also need explicit instruction in ethical AI use. Teacher preparation programs should begin discussing questions such as:

What information should never be entered into an AI system?

What counts as personally identifiable information?

How do district-approved AI tools differ from public platforms?

When should AI not be used at all?

How can educators protect student confidentiality while still benefiting from AI-supported instructional planning?

These conversations are increasingly essential components of professional preparation. If we teach preservice teachers only how to use AI tools, but not how to evaluate them responsibly, we risk normalizing unsafe instructional habits before candidates even enter the profession.

Practical Ways Teacher Educators Can Address Student Privacy

Fortunately, teacher educators do not need to redesign entire programs to begin addressing these concerns. Small instructional shifts can make a significant difference.

1. Model Safe AI Practices During Instruction

Faculty should consistently demonstrate responsible use when modeling AI tools within class. For example:

Use fictional student examples instead of real cases.

Remove identifying details from classroom scenarios.

Demonstrate how to redact information before using AI tools.

Explain why certain information should never be uploaded.

These small modeling decisions communicate professional expectations clearly and consistently.

One simple strategy is encouraging preservice teachers to ask themselves a short series of questions before uploading any materials to AI:

Does this contain identifiable student information?

Would I be comfortable sharing this publicly?

Is this tool approved by a district or institution?

Am I protecting student dignity and confidentiality?

Could this information unintentionally identify a child?

Building this reflective pause into coursework helps future educators develop habits of professional judgment rather than impulsive use of technology.

3. Incorporate AI Ethics into Assignments and Discussions

Teacher educators can integrate ethical reflection into existing coursework without sacrificing instructional time. For example:

Have students analyze AI-use scenarios for ethical concerns.

Ask candidates to identify unsafe prompting practices.

Include privacy considerations within lesson-planning assignments.

Discuss how AI intersects with professional teaching standards.

These discussions help candidates recognize that technology integration is not simply technical but also grounded in pedagogy and ethics.

4. Emphasize District Policies and Approved Platforms

Many preservice teachers assume all AI tools function similarly. They often do not understand that districts may have approved platforms with specific privacy agreements in place, a practice mandated for example, by NY Education Law §2-d. Teacher education programs should therefore help candidates understand:

The importance of district policies.

Approved educational tools.

Data protection expectations.

Professional accountability during field placements.

This is especially important as school districts continue to develop their own AI guidelines and policies.

5. Frame Student Privacy as an Issue of Trust

Perhaps most importantly, teacher educators should frame student privacy as more than compliance. At its core, protecting student information is about trust. Families trust educators with sensitive academic, health, behavioral, and personal information. Students trust teachers to handle their experiences responsibly and professionally. AI does not diminish that obligation. Rather, the rapid growth of AI tools makes this relationship of trust and corresponding ethical decision-making even more critical. Future educators must understand that innovation should never come at the expense of student dignity or confidentiality.

Preparing Teachers for Responsible AI Integration

AI will almost certainly remain a growing part of K-12 education, and teacher preparation programs have a critical opportunity to shape how future educators approach those tools. The goal should not be fear or avoidance. AI can absolutely support creativity, differentiation, organization and reformative instructional design. But responsible integration requires more than technological fluency, it requires appropriate professional judgment.

As colleges and universities prepare future teachers for AI-enhanced classrooms, student privacy cannot become an afterthought. Long after candidates forget the perfect prompt structure on the latest AI platform, they must remember a far more important lesson: each technological decision educators make should protect the trust, dignity, and well-being of the students they serve.

Dr. Richard J. Violanti is an assistant professor in the College of Education at Niagara University. He holds a PhD in Curriculum, Instruction, and the Science of Learning from SUNY Buffalo, where his research examined how teachers integrate technology using the TPACK and SAMR Frameworks.

Before joining higher education, he spent more than 31 years as a secondary social studies teacher, department chair, and instructional technology leader in New York State public schools. During that time, he led curriculum redesign initiatives, supported district technology adoption, and facilitated professional learning communities focused on instructional design and ethical technology use.

At Niagara University, Dr. Violanti teaches foundations and pedagogy courses and works to integrate AI literacy and student-centered technology practices into teacher preparation. His work focuses on helping instructors use emerging technologies in ways that strengthen relationships, deepen learning, and support all students.

title: Identity authentication and higher ed
summary: A stark reminder that identity sits at the centre of exposure to cyber risk is how recent attacks in the education sector persistently compromise vital student data – such as names, contact details, and identification numbers.
full_text:
Australian universities are under more pressure to deliver secure, frictionless digital experiences to a diverse population of students, staff, researchers, alumni and partners.

Legacy systems and homegrown authentication tools that once got the job done are now liabilities. They are costly to maintain, difficult to secure, and increasingly out of step with what a digitally fluent student cohort expects.

The sector cannot afford to get this wrong. Education remains the top five sectors by volume of data breach notifications to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC). In 2025, education accounted for over a third (36 per cent) of the data breaches reported.

A stark reminder that identity sits at the centre of exposure to cyber risk is how recent attacks in the education sector persistently compromise vital student data – such as names, contact details, and identification numbers – across education institutions globally. Having visibility over who is accessing what is no longer optional.

A newer version of the same problem is now emerging across campuses: the decentralised rollout of agentic AI. Individual faculties, research teams, and departments are using their own AI agents largely outside the visibility of central IT. These agents often hold powerful database credentials and operate at machine speed, with none of the built-in accountability a human user has.

Here are five key considerations for those rethinking their Identity and Access Management (IAM) approach.

Simplicity beats a custom build

Building a bespoke IAM system in-house is tempting, but it’s expensive to build and even more expensive to maintain over an institution's lifetime.

Before adopting our single cloud identity platform, Flinders University was running around 250 administrative systems, patched together with ageing directories, and fielding close to 3,000 password reset requests a year.

Off-the-shelf platforms that are purpose-built for educational institutions can integrate legacy, modern and cloud applications without months of custom development. Flinders now handles fewer than 400 resets annually, saving its IT team real time and budget.

The goal of an IAM is to make the technology invisible so students can focus on their studies. Flinders’ own commencement process was once so cumbersome that staff had nicknamed it ‘87 Steps to Flinders.’

After consolidating identity onto a single platform, new students, staff and casual academics can now activate their accounts in under 60 seconds, a small change that creates lasting first impressions.

Bring every division into the room early

Faculties, campuses and research units all have different identity needs, from student records, HR systems, guest researcher access, shared library to lab accounts.

Global institution the University of Notre Dame found this out by managing identity across more than a dozen distinct user types including students, faculty, alumni, donors, service accounts, shared accounts, even external researchers accessing shared file systems and library collections.

Engaging stakeholder groups from the outset, rather than retrofitting their requirements after the fact, is the key factor to a smooth rollout. In this case, it allowed the university to identify edge cases early, such as status changes like student-to-alumni transitions.

Treat security as foundational, not bolted on

Universities are prime targets for phishing and credential-based attacks, as they hold a valuable mix of student records, research data and financial information.

A modern IAM approach offers encryption, multi-factor authentication, and continuous visibility into who is accessing what, and from where. It needs to be built in from day one.

Notre Dame, migrating away from a homegrown system running more than 200 servers, discovered within the first 10 minutes of going live that its community was authenticating from more than 80 countries. The visibility had simply been unavailable under its previous fragmented set-up, and that immediately strengthened its ability to monitor and respond to unusual access patterns.

Govern AI agents like any other identity

Institutions need to get ahead of the proliferation of AI agents on campus and gain better control over what these agents can connect to and what they can do.

The modern identity security approach must govern AI agents and machine identities alongside human identities. This involves putting gates in place to discover threats operating outside sanctioned channels, scoping agent access down to only what’s necessary, and building in execution-time kill switches so a rogue or compromised agent can be shut down before it does damage.

Start small, move fast, and let your users make the case for you

Resist the urge to wait for a fully scoped perfect implementation plan otherwise there’s a risk that institutional inertia will swallow it.

Flinders rolled out its first 10 integrated applications to 38,000 users inside a 10-week window, while Notre Dame cut over 18,200 students, faculty and staff to single sign-on and adaptive multi-factor authentication in just two days, timed deliberately over a quiet weekend before the start of the academic year.

Early visible wins build the internal case and give users the confidence for the larger migrations that follow. It allows the institutions to turn their own users into advocates for further investment.

A foundation for what’s next

As the threat landscape continues to evolve, institutions are turning to unified identity platforms for discovery, access, and credential lifecycle, with the flexibility to bridge legacy environments under one roof.

For the higher education sector, it has never been more important to establish the right foundation to consolidate governance across the full campus identity landscape.

Choosing a school district means choosing much of a child’s daily life: the adults who teach them, the friends they see, and the activities they can try. California’s strongest options include both full school systems and districts that mainly serve teenagers. That difference matters when a family is planning several years ahead.

This countdown follows the first 25 districts in Niche’s 2027 California ranking, checked in October 2026.1 It is a published comparison, not an official state grade or our own measurement of teaching quality.2 Niche combines academic indicators with other school measures and survey responses.2 Each entry pairs that ranking with a district source and practical questions to help families investigate further.

Locations below identify the district’s base or communities, not guaranteed attendance boundaries. Check the exact address, school assignment, and any program application rules with the district. A higher place on this list does not establish that every campus, classroom, or service will suit every child.

25

Carlsbad Unified School District

Carlsbad, California.1

Carlsbad brings several routes through school into the same district. Its official program listings include advanced learner education, career pathways, and expanded learning, alongside its neighborhood schools.3 The appeal is having options to explore before a teenager settles on a college major or job.

Start with the career pathway list, then ask which courses run at the assigned campus. A course listed somewhere in a district does not tell you whether it fits your child’s timetable. For younger children, compare the elementary school and after-school arrangements first; those daily details matter long before college applications arrive.

Program listings include advanced learner education, career pathways, and expanded learning.

Check which pathway courses run at the assigned campus and fit the student’s schedule.

For younger children, compare elementary teaching and after-school arrangements.

24

Capistrano Unified School District

San Juan Capistrano, California.1

Capistrano’s official website gives language immersion and College and Career Advantage prominent places among its offerings.4 That makes it worth examining for families who want language study or practical career exploration within a public school system.

The next step is to follow the program, not just the district name. Ask where each option takes place, when students can enter, and how transportation works. A strong academic plan should also leave room for the arts and other interests. Capistrano publishes a high school course catalog, which gives families a useful starting point for planning that balance before registration.

District offerings include language immersion and College and Career Advantage.

A published high school course catalog helps families plan classes.

Check program locations, entry points, transportation, and room for other interests.

San Diego and Poway, California.1

Poway serves schools in both San Diego and Poway, so the name does not describe the whole footprint. The district identifies comprehensive high schools, a continuation school, and a middle college among its options.5 That range is worth a closer look when a conventional high school schedule is not the right fit.

Families should compare their assigned school with any alternative they are considering. Ask how students enter, what support they receive, and whether credits transfer cleanly. For children still in elementary school, trace the full route through middle and high school rather than judging the address by one campus.

The district serves schools in both San Diego and Poway.

Secondary options include comprehensive high schools, a continuation school, and a middle college.

Compare entry rules, student support, credit transfers, and the full school sequence.

22

Sunnyvale, California.1

This is a high school district, an important distinction for families shopping for elementary schools. Its official materials describe comprehensive campuses, career technical education, and an English learner program.6 Those offerings give teenagers different ways to prepare for study and work after graduation.

The district name can also cause confusion: it is not Fremont Unified across the bay. Check the exact address and campus assignment before making plans. Once the school is confirmed, compare its course sequence with your teenager’s current credits. Moving into a well-ranked district works better when the student can continue the subjects already underway.

This high school district is separate from Fremont Unified across the bay.

Its resources cover career technical education and English learner support.

Confirm campus assignment and how existing credits fit the school’s course sequence.

21

San Mateo, California.1

San Mateo Union’s Middle College program links high school study with the local community college district. Its enrollment information explains that students can earn college credit while meeting high school diploma requirements.7 That is a concrete option for teenagers who would benefit from a different setting.

It deserves a separate conversation from the district’s overall ranking. Ask about entry requirements, available places, supervision, and the pace of college coursework. A student who wants that independence may find it appealing; another may prefer a comprehensive campus. The useful question is which setting supports the student’s habits, interests, and readiness.

Middle College connects high school study with the local community college district.

Students can earn college credit while meeting high school diploma requirements.

Check entry rules, available places, supervision, and readiness for college coursework.

Placentia, California.1

Placentia–Yorba Linda gives families more to investigate than a test-score headline. Its official overview highlights CareerLink academies, a sustained music program, and a performing arts center.8 Together, those features suggest several directions for a child whose interests are still taking shape.

Look at the academy’s actual sequence of classes rather than treating its name as a promise of employment. Ask how students apply and whether they can keep taking music, language, or advanced academic courses at the same time. The best combination is one a teenager can complete without giving up every other interest that keeps school enjoyable.

CareerLink academies provide career-focused options to explore.

The district also highlights music programming and a performing arts center.

Check academy applications and whether course sequences leave room for other interests.

Irvine, California.1

Irvine’s official site highlights a district band event involving its comprehensive high schools, alongside academic recognition and work on belonging and bullying prevention.9 For a family with a young musician, that is a useful reason to look beyond an academic league table.

Find out how a child progresses from beginner instruction to secondary ensembles, and whether instruments or participation costs create extra demands. For other students, ask the same practical questions about their own interests. The ranking gets Irvine onto the shortlist; the child’s assigned school, support network, and chance to take part should decide whether it stays there.

Other reported work addresses belonging and bullying prevention.

Ask about beginner music instruction, later ensembles, instrument access, and participation costs.

Lafayette, California.1

Acalanes Union organizes its public information around both coursework and student support. Families can find career technical education, visual and performing arts, college and career pathways, and a wellness program.10 That combination is worth examining for teenagers who need academic challenge and accessible help.

Because this is a high school district, parents of younger children need to research their earlier school placements separately. For an incoming teenager, ask what wellness support looks like during an ordinary week. Who can a student approach, how are appointments made, and what happens when schoolwork starts to slip? Those answers make the program list more useful.

A wellness program adds another form of student support.

Pleasanton’s official information includes a dual language immersion program, performing arts, and several secondary campuses.11 This gives families a reason to compare the district’s different routes rather than assume every child follows an identical program.

Language immersion needs particular attention to entry points and continuity. Ask how it develops across grade levels and what happens if a student joins later. For high school students, review the assigned campus’s course guide and support services. A district can offer a wide menu while individual schedules remain limited, so build a realistic school week around the choices your child could actually make.

District options include dual language immersion and performing arts.

Several secondary campuses offer different routes to investigate.

Check immersion entry points, later-grade continuity, and the assigned school’s course guide.

Santa Monica–Malibu Unified School District

Santa Monica and Malibu, California.1

The district’s school directory includes separate campuses in Santa Monica and Malibu, while its program information covers visual and performing arts and career technical education.12 The geography matters: a family should not treat the two communities as one interchangeable school location.

Begin with the exact campus and daily journey, then explore the program that interests your child. Ask whether it is available locally or requires a different placement. For a teenager, compare course sequences and counseling before looking at headline achievements. That approach keeps the focus on the education the child would receive, rather than opportunities somewhere else in the district.

The district has separate campuses in Santa Monica and Malibu.

Program information covers visual and performing arts and career technical education.

Confirm the assigned campus, commute, local program access, and counseling support.

El Segundo Unified School District

El Segundo has a specific achievement behind its appeal to families interested in applied learning. In its 2026 announcement, the district reported Project Lead the Way recognition for Center Street School, Richmond Street School, and El Segundo High School.13 The recognition concerns access, participation, and achievement within those programs.

For parents, the practical question is how that classroom work develops over time. Ask what children design, test, or build at each stage, and how those projects connect with reading and mathematics. The award is a useful lead, while a school visit can show whether the teaching style suits your child’s way of learning.

Three district schools received Project Lead the Way recognition in 2026.

The recognition addresses access, participation, and achievement within those programs.

Ask what students design and build, and how projects connect with reading and math.

Piedmont Unified School District

Piedmont, California.1

Piedmont’s enrollment information describes both its comprehensive high school and Millennium, an alternative high school. It also explains that out-of-district applicants to Millennium face an application and interview process, followed by transfer paperwork if accepted.14 That detail matters more than assuming a nearby address provides access.

Families considering either route should ask how a student receives academic and personal support. For the alternative setting, discuss the student’s goals and what a typical week involves. A smaller environment can be worth exploring, but fit depends on the actual instruction, relationships, and expectations rather than the size of the school alone.

Secondary options include a comprehensive high school and Millennium alternative high school.

Out-of-district Millennium applicants must apply, interview, and complete transfer steps if accepted.

Compare daily instruction, expectations, and academic and personal support.

13

Laguna Beach Unified School District

Laguna Beach, California.1

Laguna Beach’s district site describes the learning garden at Thurston Middle School as a place connecting environmental study, nutrition, wellness, and hands-on work. It also reports a high school digital wellness initiative that invited students to reflect on their social media habits.15

Those examples give parents concrete topics for a visit. Ask how outdoor learning enters regular lessons, and how student feedback shapes wellbeing work. Neither a garden nor a short pilot proves an entire district’s quality. They do, however, show useful areas to investigate when your priorities include practical learning and a healthier relationship with technology.

Thurston Middle School’s learning garden connects environmental study, nutrition, and wellness.

A high school initiative encouraged students to reflect on social media habits.

Ask how these activities shape everyday lessons and respond to student feedback.

12

Oak Park Unified School District

Oak Park, California.1

Oak Park’s school directory includes its elementary schools, Medea Creek Middle School, Oak Park High School, and Oak View High School. The district also lists an extended-care program.16 That helps families begin mapping both the school journey and the hours around it.

Do not assume a different campus is automatically open to every student. Ask which placement rules apply and what support is available at the assigned school before exploring alternatives. For younger children, check the hours, costs, and availability of extended care. A workable daily routine can make a promising school choice much easier for the whole family to sustain.

The school directory includes Medea Creek Middle, Oak Park High, and Oak View High.

An extended-care program helps families explore care around school hours.

Confirm campus placement rules and extended-care hours, costs, and availability.

11

Carmel Unified School District

Carmel, California.1

Carmel’s official directory includes Captain Cooper and Tularcitos elementary schools, Carmel Middle School, Carmel High School, and Carmel Valley High School. Its resources also cover college and career readiness and a performing arts center.17 Families therefore have several specific campuses and programs to investigate.

Start with the child’s assigned school, particularly when comparing homes in different parts of the district. Then ask how the next transition works and which activities fit the daily journey. For a teenager, compare the high school options directly with staff. A shared district name should be the start of those conversations, not the end of them.

The directory lists elementary campuses, Carmel Middle, and two high school options.

Resources also cover college and career readiness and a performing arts center.

Check campus assignment, school transitions, and how activities fit the daily commute.

10

Los Gatos–Saratoga Union High School District

Los Gatos and Saratoga, California.1

Los Gatos–Saratoga’s official overview highlights music, student creative work, and a post-secondary program for students with disabilities.18 Those are useful reminders that a high school district’s strengths can extend beyond university admission.

A family comparing its campuses should ask how students enter ensembles, develop projects, and receive help planning the next stage of life. For a student with a disability, discuss transition goals and services directly with the school team. For younger siblings, research the separate elementary and middle school districts. The high school ranking does not automatically describe the whole educational route leading to these campuses.

A post-secondary program supports students with disabilities.

Discuss transition services with staff and research earlier school districts separately.

9

Arcadia Unified School District

Arcadia, California.1

Arcadia’s official overview describes elementary and middle schools feeding into one comprehensive high school, alongside an alternative school and outreach program. It also describes investment in classrooms, science labs, libraries, and arts facilities.19 That structure makes the transition into secondary education a central question for prospective families.

Ask how incoming students find an adviser, join activities, and receive support during the first term. A campus with many opportunities can still feel different from a child’s earlier school. For younger students, investigate their assigned elementary campus on its own merits, then look ahead to how its learning connects with the later grades.

Mountain View–Los Altos Union High School District

Mountain View–Los Altos serves Mountain View, Los Altos, and Los Altos Hills. Its official district information lists comprehensive high schools, Alta Vista, Middle College, and Freestyle Academy for Arts and Technology.20 That gives teenagers several distinct routes to investigate.

The names are a starting point; ask about entry rules, location, and how each program fits with required courses. Despite the words “High School” in its name, San Dieguito’s official information includes both middle and high schools. Families should first confirm the feeder-school route and campus assignment. Then compare the particular options available at that school, including any separate application process. San Marino’s official website lists two elementary schools, Huntington Middle School, and San Marino High School. For immersion, ask about entry grades, spaces, and how language study continues later. For the broader school experience, request examples of how cultural partnerships reach ordinary classroom work. title: La revista Tramas y Redes se incorpora al Catálogo Latindex

Sistemas de información y evaluación de revistas académicas

La entrada La revista Tramas y Redes se incorpora al Catálogo Latindex se publicó primero en CLACSO.
full_text:
La revista científica Tramas y Redes, editada por CLACSO, ha sido incorporada al Catálogo Latindex, uno de los sistemas de información y evaluación de revistas académicas más reconocidos de Iberoamérica. Este logro constituye un importante reconocimiento a la calidad editorial, la rigurosidad académica y el compromiso con la ciencia abierta que caracterizan a la publicación desde su creación.

La inclusión en Latindex representa mucho más que una indexación. Significa que la revista cumple con estándares internacionales de calidad editorial, transparencia, buenas prácticas científicas, visibilidad y accesibilidad, aspectos fundamentales para fortalecer la circulación del conocimiento producido en América Latina y el Caribe.

Tramas y Redes nació con el propósito de promover debates críticos sobre las transformaciones contemporáneas de la producción, circulación y apropiación social del conocimiento, poniendo especial atención en las desigualdades que atraviesan los sistemas científicos, tecnológicos y educativos. Desde una perspectiva regional y comprometida con el acceso abierto, la revista se ha consolidado como un espacio de reflexión e intercambio para investigadores e investigadoras, responsables de políticas públicas y actores sociales vinculados a la construcción de ecosistemas de conocimiento más democráticos e inclusivos.

La incorporación al Catálogo Latindex reafirma el trabajo sostenido de los equipos editoriales, de evaluación y de gestión que participan en la producción de la revista, así como la importancia de fortalecer infraestructuras académicas públicas, cooperativas y no comerciales para la comunicación científica.

Asimismo, este reconocimiento contribuye a ampliar la visibilidad internacional de los artículos publicados, favorece su descubrimiento por parte de nuevas comunidades académicas y fortalece la presencia de las ciencias sociales latinoamericanas en los principales circuitos de circulación del conocimiento.

En un contexto marcado por crecientes procesos de concentración y mercantilización de la comunicación científica, la incorporación de Tramas y Redes a Latindex constituye también una reafirmación del compromiso de CLACSO con la construcción de modelos editoriales de calidad, sustentados en los principios de acceso abierto, cooperación académica y conocimiento como bien común.

Este nuevo paso fortalece la proyección regional e internacional de la revista y consolida su aporte a la promoción de una ciencia más abierta, plural, democrática y socialmente comprometida.

title: Frodi nella green economy e nel PNRR, il ruolo decisivo dei dati
summary:
Green economy e PNRR concentrano risorse, accelerano procedure e ampliano i rischi di frode. Rendicontazione di sostenibilità, revisione, controlli pubblici e intelligenza artificiale diventano strumenti complementari per verificare dati, filiere e risultati, proteggendo investimenti e sicurezza economica senza confondere anomalie e prove

L'articolo Frodi nella green economy e nel PNRR, il ruolo decisivo dei dati proviene da Agenda Digitale.
full_text:
La transizione ecologica viene spesso raccontata attraverso tecnologie, obiettivi climatici e capacità di investimento. È una lettura corretta, che acquista però un significato più ampio quando si considera che ogni grande programma di trasformazione economica produce anche una nuova geografia del rischio, perché concentra risorse, accelera procedure, moltiplica i soggetti coinvolti e affida una parte crescente delle decisioni a dati che devono essere raccolti, classificati e verificati.

Nel caso del PNRR questa dinamica appare particolarmente evidente. La qualità dell’esecuzione dipende dalla capacità di collegare la spesa alla prestazione effettivamente resa, alle caratteristiche del soggetto che la realizza e al risultato che il finanziamento dovrebbe produrre.

Frodi nella green economy e nel PNRR: dimensioni e rischi

La dimensione raggiunta dal fenomeno consiglia di guardare oltre la regolarità amministrativa del singolo progetto. Nel bilancio operativo relativo al periodo compreso tra gennaio 2025 e maggio 2026, la Guardia di Finanza ha indicato 14.951 interventi sui progetti e sugli investimenti finanziati con risorse PNRR, per un valore superiore a 10,2 miliardi di euro. Sono numeri che restituiscono la misura di una questione ormai strettamente collegata alla protezione delle risorse pubbliche, alla correttezza della concorrenza e all’affidabilità delle filiere sulle quali poggiano infrastrutture, innovazione e capacità produttiva.

La transizione verde crea dunque un terreno nel quale sostenibilità e sicurezza economica tendono ad avvicinarsi. Una frode che consente di ottenere un incentivo senza possederne i requisiti, una sovrafatturazione, un subappalto opaco o una falsa rappresentazione delle prestazioni ambientali generano conseguenze che vanno ben oltre il danno patrimoniale immediato. Possono alterare il mercato, favorire operatori meno affidabili, ridurre la qualità delle opere, spostare capitale verso attività improduttive e compromettere la credibilità dell’intero meccanismo di finanziamento. Quando gli investimenti riguardano energia, reti, mobilità, edilizia, tecnologie pulite o infrastrutture critiche, la dimensione economica finisce inevitabilmente per intrecciarsi con quella strategica.

Dati di sostenibilità e prevenzione delle frodi verdi

Una parte importante della prevenzione passa dalla qualità dell’informazione. Negli ultimi anni l’Unione europea ha costruito un sistema nel quale la rendicontazione di sostenibilità è diventata progressivamente più strutturata, comparabile e sottoposta a verifica. La Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, gli European Sustainability Reporting Standards e la tassonomia europea hanno spinto le imprese a documentare in modo più rigoroso impatti, rischi, opportunità e dati ambientali lungo il perimetro aziendale e, in misura crescente, lungo la catena del valore.

Nel corso del 2026 questo impianto è stato sensibilmente ricalibrato, la Direttiva (UE) 2026/470 ha ridotto il numero delle imprese comprese nel perimetro degli obblighi e ha semplificato diversi passaggi della disciplina, mentre il successivo Regolamento delegato (UE) 2026/1563 ha rivisto gli ESRS, riducendo gli elementi informativi meno rilevanti e concentrando maggiormente l’attenzione sui dati effettivamente utili. Il nuovo quadro europeo dovrà essere recepito negli ordinamenti nazionali secondo le tempistiche previste, e proprio questa fase di transizione suggerisce di distinguere con attenzione tra adempimento formale e valore sostanziale dell’informazione.

Quando un dato di sostenibilità viene utilizzato per orientare capitale, dimostrare il raggiungimento di un obiettivo, accedere a un finanziamento o sostenere la credibilità di un investimento, la sua attendibilità assume infatti un valore economico autonomo. La sostenibilità dovrebbe per questo essere letta sempre meno come linguaggio reputazionale e sempre più come infrastruttura informativa, nella quale la qualità di un dato sulle emissioni, sul consumo energetico, sulla provenienza dei materiali o sulle performance di filiera dipende da procedure, responsabilità, sistemi di raccolta e controlli interni che devono poter essere ricostruiti.

La precisione apparente di una percentuale o di un indicatore offre poche garanzie quando il processo che l’ha generato resta opaco. Il valore dell’informazione nasce dalla possibilità di comprenderne l’origine, verificare le assunzioni utilizzate, individuare chi l’abbia validata e ricostruire il modo in cui siano state gestite eventuali discrepanze. È una questione che interessa direttamente le imprese, ma riguarda allo stesso tempo investitori, amministrazioni, soggetti finanziatori e tutti coloro che assumono decisioni sulla base di quelle informazioni.

Il revisore della sostenibilità nella prevenzione delle frodi

Diretta conseguenza di queste premesse è che oggi assume particolare rilievo il ruolo del revisore della sostenibilità. Il decreto legislativo 6 settembre 2024, n. 125, ha dato attuazione in Italia alla CSRD e ha definito il sistema nazionale della rendicontazione e della relativa attestazione. Il quadro europeo è oggi interessato dalle modifiche introdotte nel 2026, che richiederanno un conseguente adeguamento nazionale, mentre resta centrale il principio secondo cui le informazioni di sostenibilità rilevanti devono poggiare su processi verificabili e su un’attività di assurance svolta secondo requisiti di competenza, indipendenza e qualità.

L’attività del revisore mantiene confini precisi, egli non dispone di poteri investigativi e l’attestazione rilasciata sulla rendicontazione non rappresenta una certificazione generale della legalità dell’impresa. Sovrapporre i due piani finirebbe per indebolire tanto la funzione di revisione quanto quella delle autorità pubbliche. Il contributo del revisore nasce piuttosto dalla valutazione della materialità, dall’esame delle evidenze, dallo scetticismo professionale e dalla verifica della coerenza tra dati, documenti e processi, attività attraverso le quali possono emergere incongruenze meritevoli di approfondimento e possono essere rafforzati i meccanismi con cui le informazioni vengono prodotte.

Questa funzione acquista maggiore rilievo quando i dati di sostenibilità derivano da processi complessi, da stime o da informazioni ricevute da soggetti terzi. Una catena del valore articolata può generare dati che attraversano fornitori, subappaltatori, piattaforme tecnologiche e sistemi di misurazione differenti. Più aumenta la distanza tra il fatto economico o ambientale e il soggetto che lo rappresenta nella rendicontazione, maggiore diventa l’esigenza di tracciabilità. Il revisore deve essere messo nella condizione di comprendere il percorso seguito dall’informazione e valutare se le assunzioni utilizzate siano ragionevoli, se il perimetro sia coerente nel tempo e se le evidenze raccolte risultino adeguate rispetto al rischio.

Lo standard ISSA 5000 per l’assurance di sostenibilità

A questa evoluzione si aggiunge l’International Standard on Sustainability Assurance 5000, destinato a divenire efficace dal 15 dicembre 2026 e concepito come riferimento internazionale per gli incarichi di assurance sulla sostenibilità. Anche in questo caso il baricentro resta nella qualità del processo, la credibilità della rendicontazione dipende dalla possibilità di sottoporre a verifica il modo in cui l’informazione è stata costruita, documentata e controllata, più che dalla semplice presenza di un documento finale formalmente completo.

Controlli sul PNRR e tutela degli interessi economici nazionali

Il PNRR mostra con particolare chiarezza quanto sia limitante considerare il controllo come una verifica documentale della spesa. Il dato finanziario deve poter essere collegato all’oggetto del contratto, all’avanzamento fisico, alla prestazione ricevuta e al soggetto che ne beneficia. La ricostruzione della catena che unisce programmazione, affidamento, esecuzione, fatturazione e risultato costituisce uno dei presupposti per individuare scostamenti che, isolatamente considerati, potrebbero apparire poco significativi.

Una società priva di una struttura operativa coerente con l’importo dell’appalto, una concentrazione anomala degli affidamenti, variazioni frequenti nella catena di subappalto, rapporti ricorrenti tra amministratori e fornitori, fatture che si susseguono con tempistiche scarsamente compatibili con l’avanzamento dei lavori oppure indicatori ambientali che migliorano senza una corrispondente evoluzione dei processi produttivi, rappresentano segnali che possono giustificare un approfondimento.

La loro presenza richiede però prudenza interpretativa, perché la distinzione tra anomalia, rilievo professionale e prova deve rimanere netta. Un sistema di prevenzione efficace deve essere capace di selezionare il rischio senza trasformare la probabilità in un giudizio anticipato.

La tutela degli interessi economici nazionali si posiziona precisamente in questo spazio, perché proteggere risorse pubbliche e investimenti significa preservare condizioni di concorrenza, qualità delle infrastrutture, continuità delle filiere e capacità del sistema produttivo di utilizzare il capitale in modo efficiente. La sicurezza economica richiede trasparenza proprietaria, affidabilità delle controparti, conoscenza delle dipendenze strategiche e capacità di comprendere dove si concentrino le vulnerabilità, nel rispetto delle regole del mercato e delle competenze attribuite dall’ordinamento ai diversi soggetti pubblici.

Questa prospettiva permette anche di comprendere perché la sostenibilità debba essere considerata parte della governance economica. Un investimento verde realizzato attraverso filiere opache o sulla base di informazioni difficilmente verificabili può raggiungere formalmente un target e generare, nello stesso tempo, inefficienze, nuove dipendenze o rischi che emergeranno soltanto in una fase successiva. La qualità del controllo consiste allora nella capacità di verificare la coerenza tra destinazione delle risorse e risultato dichiarato, individuando tempestivamente gli scostamenti senza produrre un rallentamento indiscriminato dell’esecuzione.

Dati e intelligenza artificiale contro le frodi nella green economy

La quantità di informazioni oggi disponibile rende sempre più difficile affidare la prevenzione a verifiche esclusivamente manuali. Contratti, fatture, assetti societari, titolarità effettive, subappalti, pagamenti, dati ambientali e indicatori di avanzamento possono essere messi in relazione attraverso tecniche di data analytics capaci di far emergere pattern anomali e collegamenti difficili da individuare attraverso una lettura tradizionale dei singoli documenti.

L’intelligenza artificiale amplia ulteriormente queste possibilità. I modelli possono supportare la classificazione documentale, estrarre informazioni da grandi quantità di testi, confrontare dichiarazioni prodotte in periodi diversi, evidenziare incoerenze, ricostruire relazioni societarie e attribuire priorità agli approfondimenti. full_text:
Proba de evaluare a competențelor din cadrul concursului pentru ocuparea funcției de director/director adjunct în unitățile de învățământ preuniversitar de stat s-a desfășurat astăzi, 13 octombrie 2026, în 42 de centre de concurs (în municipiul București au fost organizate două centre).

Proba a constat în rezolvarea, de către candidați, în maximum 60 de minute, a unui test standardizat cu 20 de itemi, fiecare item (0,5p) având 4 variante de răspuns și un singur răspuns corect.

Subiectele au fost elaborate de Centrul Național pentru Curriculum și Evaluare (CNCE), au vizat situații ipotetice din activitatea curentă a unei școli și au inclus: 7 itemi de raționament verbal (capacitatea de a utiliza eficient vocabularul pentru a înțelege sau transmite clar concepte și perspective), 7 itemi de raționament numeric (abilitatea de a înțelege informațiile numerice și de a rezolva corect problemele matematice) și 6 itemi de raționament logic (abilitatea de a înțelege ideile exprimate cu ajutorul logicii și rațiunii).

Nota minimă pentru promovarea acestei probe este 6. Nota obținută nu se include în media finală. Nota obținută poate fi contestată în termen de 24 de ore de la comunicarea rezultatelor.

Evaluarea s-a realizat digitalizat, pe platforma dedicată.

Datele extrase din platforma de evaluare digitalizată relevă următoarele rezultate, înainte de contestații:

*Excluzând candidații înscriși și validați în județul Buzău

Din 6.841 de candidați înscriși și validați (excluzând candidații înscriși și validați în județul Buzău), au fost prezenți 6.684 (97,7%).

4.615 (69,05%) dintre candidații prezenți au obținut cel puțin nota 6 și vor putea participa la următoarele etape ale concursului.

Distribuția pe note

Rata de promovare pe județe

Cea mai mare rată de promovare se înregistrează în categoria de vârstă 40-44 de ani.

Proba de evaluare a competențelor din cadrul concursului pentru ocuparea funcției de director/director adjunct în unitățile de învățământ preuniversitar de stat s-a desfășurat astăzi, 13 octombrie 2026, în 42 de centre de concurs (în municipiul București au fost organizate două centre).

Proba a constat în rezolvarea, de către candidați, în maximum 60 de minute, a unui test standardizat cu 20 de itemi, fiecare item (0,5p) având 4 variante de răspuns și un singur răspuns corect.

Subiectele au fost elaborate de Centrul Național pentru Curriculum și Evaluare (CNCE), au vizat situații ipotetice din activitatea curentă a unei școli și au inclus: 7 itemi de raționament verbal (capacitatea de a utiliza eficient vocabularul pentru a înțelege sau transmite clar concepte și perspective), 7 itemi de raționament numeric (abilitatea de a înțelege informațiile numerice și de a rezolva corect problemele matematice) și 6 itemi de raționament logic (abilitatea de a înțelege ideile exprimate cu ajutorul logicii și rațiunii).

Nota minimă pentru promovarea acestei probe este 6. Nota obținută nu se include în media finală. Nota obținută poate fi contestată în termen de 24 de ore de la comunicarea rezultatelor.

Evaluarea s-a realizat digitalizat, pe platforma dedicată.

Datele extrase din platforma de evaluare digitalizată relevă următoarele rezultate, înainte de contestații:

*Excluzând candidații înscriși și validați în județul Buzău

Din 6.841 de candidați înscriși și validați (excluzând candidații înscriși și validați în județul Buzău), au fost prezenți 6.684 (97,7%).

4.615 (69,05%) dintre candidații prezenți au obținut cel puțin nota 6 și vor putea participa la următoarele etape ale concursului.
